rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters claimed idols brought them near God; recognizing that the idols themselves depend on God invalidates their divinity.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يقولون: إن الأصنام تقربهم إلى الله فإذا علموا أنها تحتاج إلى الله فقد بطل كونها آلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links the wording to the verse about those invoked seeking a means to their Lord and competing to be nearest.
rows.anchor: كقوله أولئك الذين يدعون يبتغون إلى ربهم الوسيلة أيهم أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf in kamā is accusative; al-Ḥawfī attaches it to the same governing relation as maʿa, the existential phrase with kāna.
rows.anchor: متعلقة بما تعلقت به مع وهو الاستقرار ومعه خبر كان

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqā construes the phrase as a verbal noun meaning your assertion.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: كونا لقولكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes idhan to mark what follows as the answer to the polytheists’ statement and the consequence of a hypothetical condition.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وإذا دالة على أن ما بعدها وهو لابتغوا جواب عن مقالة المشركين وجزاء للو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʿālā is coordinated with subḥānahu, a noun standing for a verbal noun; the preposition ʿan can govern both by shared construction.
rows.anchor: وعطف وتعالى على قوله سبحانه لأنه اسم قام مقام المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine transcendence here concerns rank and status, not location.
rows.anchor: والتعالي في حقه تعالى هو بالمكانة لا بالمكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisāʾī read the verb with second-person tāʾ; the other seven readers use third-person yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان: عما تقولون بالتاء من فوق وباقي السبعة بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUlūwan is a verbal noun in a different form from the verb, while takbīran intensifies the disavowal and distance from their attribution.
rows.anchor: وانتصب علوا على أنه مصدر على غير الصدر أي تعاليا ووصف تكبيرا مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The incompatibility between necessary and contingent, eternal and originated, and self-sufficient and needy admits no increase; takbīran is emphatic hyperbole.
rows.anchor: منافاة لا تقبل الزيادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes the heavens, earth, and their inhabitants as literally uttering glorification, with God granting speech even to things without life or growth.
rows.anchor: حمله بعضهم على النطق بالتسبيح حقيقة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says living creatures glorify literally: a tree does so, but a column does not.
rows.anchor: وبه قال عكرمة قال: الشجرة تسبح والأسطوانة لا تسبح

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a wooden dining tray once glorified when it was a tree, but ceased when it became dead wood.
rows.anchor: وسئل الحسن عن الخوان أيسبح؟ فقال: قد كان تسبح مرة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view reads the glorification of inanimate things metaphorically: their condition points to the Maker, power, wisdom, and perfection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التسبيح المنسوب لما لا يعقل مجاز ومعناه أنها تسبح بلسان الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address that people do not understand the glorification targets polytheists: their acknowledgment of God as Creator is contradicted by their associating other gods.
rows.anchor: ويكون قوله: ولكن لا تفقهون تسبيحهم خطابا للمشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A metaphorical account can apply commonly to all creation, while angels, humans, and jinn also glorify literally; he avoids assigning metaphor and literal meaning to the same word at once.
rows.anchor: فيكون التسبيح المسند إلى السموات والأرض ومن فيهن على سبيل المجاز قدرا مشتركا بين الجميع

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the relative pronoun man treats heavens and earth as rational because glorification is predicated of them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية ثم أعاد على السموات والأرض ضمير من يعقل لما أسند إليها فعل العاقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s assumption that hun is limited to rational feminine plurals; it can refer broadly to feminine plurals.
rows.anchor: وليس كما تخيل بل هن يكون ضمير الجمع المؤنث مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two grammarians, Ḥamza, and Ḥafṣ read tasbaḥ with tāʾ; the remaining seven read yasbaḥ with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النحويان وحزة وحفص: تسبح بالتاء من فوق وباقي السبعة بالياء

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: The codex reading attributed to ʿAbd Allāh, al-Aʿmash, and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif has the feminine past-tense form sabbaḥat.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض المصاحف سبحت له السموات بلفظ الماضي وتاء التأنيث وهي قراءة عبد الله والأعمش وطلحة بن مصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is forbearing by delaying punishment for their bad judgment, and forgiving if they return and affirm divine unity.
rows.anchor: إنه كان حليما حيث لا يعاجلكم بالعقوبة على سوء نظركم غفورا إن رجعتم ووحدتم الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the barrier verse was revealed about Abū Sufyān, al-Naḍr, Abū Jahl, and Umm Jamīl, who harassed the Prophet when he recited; God obscured his sight from them.
rows.anchor: فكانوا يمرون به ولا يرونه قاله الكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās recounts Umm Jamīl confronting Abū Bakr with a stone over the satire about her necklace; the Prophet said an angel continually screened him, and she could not see him.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس نزلت في امرأة أبي لهب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says men of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār harassed him at night as he prayed and recited aloud, and God kept them from harming him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت في قوم من بني عبد الدار كانوا يؤذونه في الليل إذا صلى وجهر بالقراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing divine unity, the passage turns to prophethood and the disbelievers’ denial of it and of resurrection.
rows.anchor: ولما تقدم الكلام في تقرير الإلهية جاء بعده تقرير النبوة وذكر شيء من أحوال الكفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means when one begins reading, not after finishing; Quran here may mean any portion bearing that name.
rows.anchor: والمعنى وإذا شرعت في القراءة وليس المعنى على الفراغ من القراءة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A view identifies the recitation as three particular passages: from al-Naḥl, al-Kahf, and al-Jāthiya.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ثلاث آيات منه معينة وهي في النحل أولئك الذين طبع

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb reports that the Prophet screened himself with those verses.
rows.anchor: وعن كعب أن الرسول كان يستتر بهذه الآيات

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sīrīn says a voice from the side of the house identified the verses for him.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن سيرين أنه عينها له هاتف من جانب البيت

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī adds the opening of Yā Sīn: during the Hijra, the Prophet scattered dust over the attackers while reciting it, and they did not see him.
rows.anchor: قال القرطبي: ويزاد إلى هذه الآي أول يس إلى فهم لا يبصرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning, supported by the occasion report, is a barrier between the Prophet’s sight and the eyes of those who reject the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المعنى جعلنا بين رؤيتك وبين أبصار الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda, al-Zajjāj, and others understand the barrier as blocking comprehension of the recitation, so they reject prophethood and resurrection; this resembles the next verse.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة والزجاج وجماعة ما معناه: جعلنا بينك فهم ما تقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mastūr apparently means screened from the disbelievers’ eyes or a screen that covers the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والظاهر إقرار مستورا على موضوعه من كونه اسم مفعول أي مستورا عن أعين الكفار

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains mastūr as what is screened with or possessing a covering, like words meaning endowed with milk or dates.
rows.anchor: ونسب الستر إليه لما كان مستورا به قاله المبرد، ويؤول معناه إلى أنه ذو ستر

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and others take mastūr to mean sāṭir, an active meaning expressed with a passive participle form.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش وجماعة مستورا ساترا واسم الفاعل قد يجيء بلفظ المفعول

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view treats mastūr as an intensive adjective, but the author objects that intensification uses an active participle derived from the same word.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مستور وصف على جهة المبالغة كما قالوا شعر شاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The veils over hearts were explained earlier in Sūrat al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا على قلوبهم أكنة أن يفقهوه وفي آذانهم وقرا تقدم تفسيره في أوائل الأنعام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says Quraysh notables visiting Abū Ṭālib heard the Prophet recite monotheism and invite them to proclaim it; they fled, prompting the verse.
rows.anchor: قيل: دخل ملأ قريش على أبي طالب يزورونه، فدخل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse apparently concerns their flight during his recitation of divine unity, in rejection and revulsion at abandoning their idols.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الآية في حال الفارين عند وقت قراءته ومروره بتوحيد الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī analyzes waḥdahu as a verbal noun standing in for a circumstantial accusative, originally meaning uniquely or alone.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وحد يحد وحدا وحدة نحو وعد يعد وعدا وعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against al-Zamakhsharī, Sībawayh says waḥdahu is a noun substituting for a verbal noun that itself substitutes for a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: خلاف مذهب سيبويه ووحده عند سيبويه ليس مصدرا بل هو اسم وضع موضع المصدر

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus construes waḥdahu as an adverbial expression.
rows.anchor: وذهب يونس إلى أن وحده منصوب على الظرف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other grammarians call waḥdahu a verbal noun with no verb, a form of awḥada with the augment removed, or a verbal noun of waḥḥada.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم إلى أنه مصدر لا فعل له، وقوم إلى أنه مصدر لأوحد على حذف الزيادة

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: After a transitive verb, Sībawayh makes waḥdahu a circumstantial accusative of the subject; al-Mubarrad also permits it to describe the object.
rows.anchor: وإذا ذكرت وحده بعد فاعل ومفعول نحو ضربت زيدا فمذهب سيبويه أنه حال من الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nufūran is either the plural of nāfir or a verbal noun in a different form, since wallaw means they fled.
rows.anchor: ونفورا حال جمع نافر كقاعد وقعود، أو مصدر على غير الصدر لأن معنى ولوا نفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in wallaw apparently refers to the previously mentioned disbelievers.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عود الضمير في ولوا على الكفار المتقدم ذكرهم

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group instead takes the pronoun as the devils, understood from the sense though not previously named.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: هو ضمير الشياطين لأنهم يفرون من القرآن دل على ذلك المعنى

rows.speaker: أبو الحوراء أوس بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥawrāʾ says nothing drives Satan from the heart more than the declaration there is no god but God, then recites this verse.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحوراء أوس بن عبد الله: ليس شيء أطرد للشيطان من القلب من لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn identifies the phrase with the basmala.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن الحسين: هو البسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They listen with mockery, derision, and idle talk; while the Prophet recited, men clapped, whistled, and mixed in poetry to disrupt him.
rows.anchor: نحن أعلم بما يستمعون به أي بالاستخفاف الذي يستمعون به والهزء بك واللغو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When knowledge or ignorance verbs take the elative or comparative pattern, they govern bi rather than the li used by other transitive verbs.
rows.anchor: وما كان في معنى العلم والجهل وإن كان متعديا لمفعول بنفسه فإنه إذا كان في باب أفعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī makes bi-hi circumstantial, construes the first idh as the time of listening, and treats the next idh as explaining the secret conversation.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī says the bi and ilā show that their listening is ridicule aimed at finding a slip or fault to attack, not simply understanding the recitation.
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفي: لم يقل يستمعونه ولا يستمعونك لما كان الغرض ليس الإخبار عن الاستماع فقط

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqā suggests bi means li, idh is temporal to the first listening, najwā is a verbal noun or plural of najī, and the following idh may be an appositive or an imperative to recall.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: يستمعون به.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya refers the pronoun in bihi to the relative ma, meaning their constant mockery and avoidance, and places the temporal construction with the first listening.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: الضمير في به عائد على ما هو بمعنى الذي، والمراد الاستخفاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr says he cannot understand what the Prophet is saying.
rows.anchor: ما أفهم ما تقول، وقال أبو سفيان

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان
rows.claim: Abū Sufyān says that some of the recitation is true.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو سفيان: أرى بعضه حقا

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Abū Jahl calls the Prophet mad.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جهل: مجنون

rows.speaker: أبو لهب
rows.claim: Abū Lahab calls him a soothsayer.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو لهب: كاهن

rows.speaker: حويطب
rows.claim: Ḥuwayṭib calls him a poet.
rows.anchor: وقال حويطب: شاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others call the recitation tales of the ancients or claim a human teaches him.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أساطير الأولين، وبعضهم إنما يعلمه بشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report places the private conversation at ʿUtba’s meal for Quraysh leaders, where they called the Prophet a sorcerer and madman.
rows.anchor: وروي أن تناجيهم كان عند عتبة دعا أشراف قريش إلى طعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense of masḥūran is a person whose mind magic has impaired.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن مسحورا من السحر أي خبل عقله السحر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says it means deceived or duped, citing the phrase asking how people are deceived.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: مخدوعا نحو فأنى تسحرون أي تخدعون

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says masḥūr means having lungs: he needs food and drink and is human rather than an angel; Arabs also use it of any creature that eats or drinks.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: مسحورا معناه أن له سحرا أي رئة فهو لا يستغني عن الطعام والشراب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites Arabic usage of a coward’s lung swelling and a poem where people are nourished or sustained by food and drink.
rows.anchor: وتقول العرب للجبان: قد انتفخ سحره ولكل من أكل أو شرب

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba objects that Abū ʿUbayda’s strained interpretation ignores the clear explanations transmitted from the early authorities.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة: لا أدري ما الذي حمل أبا عبيدة على هذا التفسير المستكره

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the next verse’s simile supports the word’s derivation from magic with kasra; the lung or nourishment sense would describe literal humanity, not a simile.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: الآية التي بعد هذا تقوي أن اللفظة من السحر بكسر السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They used the labels to console and mislead one another; al-Walīd judged sorcerer most persuasive to newcomers, leaving them unable to find a path to faith or to undermine God’s light.
rows.anchor: ثم رأى الوليد بن المغيرة أن أقر بها لتخييل الطارئين عليهم هو أنه ساحر

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the passage was revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and his companions; they marvel at and deny resurrection after becoming bones and fragments.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري أنها نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة وأصحابه وقالوا: أإذا كنا هذا استفهام تعجب وإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answers that He first brought them into being from nothing; a reading that looks declarative still implies a question, with the interrogative hamza elided.
rows.anchor: ولكنه حذف همزة الاستفهام لدلالة المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional phrase omits its apodosis, ‘if we are bones and dust, are we raised?’; Sībawayh and Yūnus differ about which omitted element the question governs.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف تقديره إذا كنا ترابا وعظاما نبعث أو نعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalqan jadīdan is a circumstantial expression whose original verbal noun is applied to the created object.
rows.anchor: وخلقا حال وهو في الأصل مصدر أطلق على المفعول أي مخلوقا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash glosses bakhiʿ as exhausting or destroying oneself through intense grief; its root sense is exertion.
rows.anchor: بخع يبخع بخعا وبخوعا أهلك من شدة الوجد وأصله الجهد قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: In a report about ʿUmar, ʿĀʾisha says he exhausted the land by taking the wealth of kings.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث عائشة ذكرت عمر فقالت: بخع الأرض أي جهدها حتى أخذ ما فيها

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī says cultivating land repeatedly makes it weak.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: بخع الأرض بالزراعة جعلها ضعيفة بسبب متابعة الحراثة

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says bakhaʿa himself means to kill oneself from grief.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: بخع الرجل نفسه قتلها من شدة وجده

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda cites al-Farazdaq’s line as evidence for bakhiʿ al-wajd, a person consuming himself in grief over what fate took away.
rows.anchor: ألا أيهذا الباخع الوجد نفسه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says Dhū al-Rumma recited al-wajd with nominative case; al-Aṣmaʿī insists on the accusative, making it a motive of action.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: كان ذو الرمة ينشد الوجد بالرفع. وقال الأصمعي: إنما هو الوجد بالفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurz describes land stripped by drought, locusts, or similar causes, left without vegetation; a barren year is called jarz, and a woman who eats much is jawz.
rows.anchor: سنة جرز وسنون أجراز لا مطر فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line about an old gluttonous woman illustrates jawz as voracious.
rows.anchor:
قال الشاعر:
إن العجوز خبة جروزا ... تأكل كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kahf is a broad opening in a mountain; if it is not broad, it is a ghār or cave. Ibn al-Anbārī reports the lexicographers’ equivalent gloss.
rows.anchor: الكهف النقب المتسع في الجبل فإن لم يك واسعا فهو غار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raqīm is on the faʿīl pattern and can mean either something inscribed or an inscriber; explanations are deferred to the exegetes’ disagreements.
rows.anchor: الرقيم: فعيل من رقم إما بمعنى مفعول وإما بمعنى فاعل

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s poem uses al-raqīm for the dog.
rows.anchor: فعني به كلبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥṣā means to preserve and record accurately.
rows.anchor: أحصى الشيء حفظه وضبطه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shaṭaṭ means injustice, exceeding a limit, and going to extremes; al-Farrāʾ also gives related lexical forms for excess, distance, wronging, and height.
rows.anchor: الشطط: الجور وتعدي الحد والغلو. وقال الفراء: اشتط في الشؤم جاوز القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tazāwar means turn away or incline; al-Akhfash glosses it as withdrawing, and azwar can describe an eye or anything that leans.
rows.anchor: تزور: تروع وتميل. وقال الأخفش: تزور تنقبض

rows.speaker: ابن أبي ربيعة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Rabīʿa’s verse witnesses the use of azwar for one who leans or turns aside.
rows.anchor: قال ابن أبي ربيعة: وجبني خيفة القوم أزوره

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: ʿAntara’s line uses azwar for turning aside from a spear’s impact.
rows.anchor: وقال عنترة: فازور من وقع القنا بلبانه

rows.speaker: بشر بن أبي حازم
rows.claim: Bishr ibn Abī Ḥāzim’s verse witnesses the noun azwirār for a directional deviation.
rows.anchor: وقال بشر بن أبي حازم: تؤم بها الحداة مياه نخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaraḍa means cut off; Kufans instead say it can mean to approach or move alongside a place, citing Bedouin usage.
rows.anchor: قرض الشيء قطعه، تقول العرب

rows.speaker: الكوفيون
rows.claim: The Kufans report Arabs saying qaraḍtahu qablan wa-dabran for approaching something from its front and back.
rows.anchor: وقال الكوفيون: قرضت موضع كذا جاذبته، وحكوا عن العرب قرضته قبلا ودبرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajwa is an open space, from a root describing separation between the thighs; fajāʾ is its plural.
rows.anchor: الفجوة: المتسع من الفجاء وهو تباعد ما بين الفخذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqiẓ means alert; its plurals include ayqāẓ and yiqāẓ, and related masculine and feminine forms are given.
rows.anchor: المتنبه وجمعه أيقاظ كعضد وأعضاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waṣīd means the courtyard, threshold, or door; the cited poem illustrates the term.
rows.anchor: الوصيد الفناء. وقيل: العتبة. وقيل: الباب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warq means silver, whether minted or unminted.
rows.anchor: الورق الفضة مضروبة وغير مضروبة

rows.speaker: أبو منصور الجواليقي
rows.claim: Abū Manṣūr al-Jawālīqī says surādiq is a Persian loan, originally sarādār meaning vestibule or passageway.
rows.anchor: قال أبو منصور الجواليقي: هو فارسي معرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq’s line uses sarādiq for an enclosure before combat.
rows.anchor: تركت لهم قبل الضراب السرادقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mahl is molten mineral material; another view takes it as the dregs of oil. Shawa is meat cooked without broth.
rows.anchor: ما أذيب من جواهر الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suwār is an arm ornament; plural forms include aswira, asāwir, and asāwīr, with Abu ʿUbayda giving aswār and Abu ʿUbayda with Quṭrub deriving asāwīr by removing an augment.
rows.anchor: السوار: ما جعل في الذراع من ذهب أو فضة أو نحاس

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī’s poem about children and poverty illustrates the form aswār for arm jewelry.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن الأنباري: والله لولا صبية صغار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sundus is fine brocade and istabraq is thick; istabraq is said to be Persian, with its final h changed to q, or associated with baraq, or simply a word for silk.
rows.anchor: السندس رقيق الديباج، والإستبرق ما غلظ منه، والإستبرق رومي عرب

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba derives istabraq from a Persian form whose h was replaced by qāf.
rows.anchor: وأصله استبره أبدلوا الهاء قافا قاله ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: المرقش
rows.claim: Al-Muraqqish’s poem witnesses the use of istabraq for brocade worn on occasion.
rows.anchor: وقال المرقش: تراهن يلبسن المشاعر مرة

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Baḥr defines istabraq as fabric woven with gold.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر: الإستبرق المنسوج بالذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arīka is a bed inside a canopy; standing alone it is not called an arīka. Al-Zajjāj glosses plural arāʾik as couches in curtained rooms.
rows.anchor: الأريكة السرير في حجلة، فإن كان وحده فلا يسمى أريكة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda consider the verse commanding patience with the worshippers a Medinan exception to the otherwise Meccan sura.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس وقتادة إلا قوله واصبر نفسك الآية فمدنية

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil regards the opening through the verse ending juruzan and the verses about believers who do good deeds as Medinan exceptions.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: إلا من أولها إلى جرزا ومن قوله إن الذين آمنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh sent al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and ʿUqba ibn Abī Muʿayṭ to Jewish scholars, who proposed questions about the youths, a world-traveling man, and the spirit as a test of Muhammad’s prophethood.
rows.anchor: وسبب نزولها أن قريشا بعثت النضر بن الحارث وعقبة بن أبي معيط إلى أحبار اليهود بالمدينة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A second report says the Jews judged that answering all three questions would disprove prophethood, while answering two and withholding the other would confirm it.
rows.anchor: وروي في هذا السبب أن اليهود قالت: إن أجابكم عن الثلاثة فليس بنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet said he would answer the next day without saying if God wills; revelation paused fifteen days, prompting Meccan rumors that his jinn inspiration had left him, then came with the answers and more.
rows.anchor: فقال: «غدا أخبركم» ولم يقل إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura’s opening connects to the prior sura’s affirmation of true revelation and humility: praise God for the upright warning Quran, which warns those asserting a son and promises believers reward.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة أول هذه السورة لآخر ما قبلها أنه لما قال وبالحق أنزلناه وبالحق نزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from direct address in the preceding sura to ‘His servant’ honors the Prophet through possessive attribution; the wording does not say ‘sent down upon you.’
rows.anchor: والتفت من الخطاب في قوله وكبره تكبيرا إلى الغيبة في قوله على عبده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One explanation says qayyiman confirms that the book is perfectly straight, an interpretation also attributed to al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
rows.anchor: وقيما تأكيد لإثبات الاستقامة إن كان مدلوله مستقيما وهو قول ابن عباس والضحاك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations make the Quran upright in people’s welfare, religious laws, and worldly and afterlife affairs, or an authority that confirms prior books.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قيما بمصالح العباد وشرائع دينهم وأمور معاشهم ومعادهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī coordinates the negated clause with ‘sent down,’ placing it inside the relative clause; then qayyiman is governed by an omitted verb to avoid separating a circumstantial from its owner.
rows.anchor: فزعم الزمخشري أنها معطوفة على أنزل فهي داخلة في الصلة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya makes qayyiman a circumstantial of the book, semantically advanced, with the negation interposed; alternatively an omitted verb governs it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: قيما نصب على الحال من الكتاب فهو بمعنى التقديم مؤخر في اللفظ

rows.speaker: العسكري
rows.claim: Al-ʿAskarī proposes fronting and postponement: praise God for the upright Quran without crookedness, since eloquence puts the most important point first.
rows.anchor: وقال العسكري: في الآية تقديم وتأخير

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says ‘no crookedness’ establishes the Quran’s perfection in itself and ‘upright’ its perfection for others; he rejects the proposed inversion as rationally impossible.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: ولم يجعل له عوجا يدل على كونه مكملا في ذاته

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmānī says the apparent analysis has two circumstantials of one book: first a clause, then a single word, without any inversion.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: إذا جعلته حالا وهو الأظهر فليس فيه تقديم ولا تأخير

rows.speaker: الأصبهاني
rows.claim: Al-Aṣbahānī favors two sequential circumstantials, meaning the book was made neither crooked nor anything but upright.
rows.anchor: واختاره الأصبهاني وقال: هما حالان متواليان والتقدير غير جاعل له عوجا قيما

rows.speaker: صاحب حل العقد
rows.claim: The author of Ḥall al-ʿIqd allows qayyiman as a single-word substitute for the entire negated clause; he notes a grammatical dispute over such substitution.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب حل العقد: يمكن أن يكون قوله قيما بدلا من قوله ولم يجعل له عوجا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qayyiman may instead describe the attached pronoun in lahu as either a stable or temporary state; the pronoun apparently refers to the book, though some refer it to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في له عائد على الكتاب وعليه التخاريج الإعرابية السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥafṣ pauses lightly after ʿiwajan before qayyiman; a Companion codex’s added ‘but made it upright’ is a gloss, not a Quranic reading.
rows.anchor: وحفص يسكت على قوله عوجا سكتة خفيفة ثم يقول قيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anẓara governs two objects; the first, those warned, is omitted initially, then stated when the warning is repeated, while the warned-against thing is supplied across the two clauses by ellipsis.
rows.anchor: حذف هنا المفعول الأول وصرح بالمنذر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because glad tidings are not repeated, both recipient and good news are named; li-yundhira apparently attaches to anzala, though al-Ḥawfī attaches it to qayyiman.
rows.anchor: ولما لم يكرر البشارة أتى بالمبشر والمبشر به

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies ‘the world’ as the omitted object of li-yundhira; Abū al-Baqā suggests servants or you, and al-Zamakhsharī says disbelievers.
rows.anchor: المحذوف قدره ابن عطية لينذر العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe warning is the afterlife’s punishment, possibly including punishment in this world.
rows.anchor: والبأس الشديد عذاب الآخرة ويحتمل أن يندرج فيه ما يلحقهم من عذاب الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min ladunhu means originating from God; Abū Bakr reads the dāl with sukun and lip-rounding, then nūn kasra, as discussed under Hūd.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر بسكون الدال وإشمامها الضم وكسر النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read yubashshiru in the indicative; the majority read it in the accusative coordinated with li-yundhira.
rows.anchor: وقرىء ويبشر بالرفع والجمهور بالنصب عطفا على لينذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good reward is Paradise; makithīn is a circumstantial of the pronoun in lahum, and abadan specifies eternity because remaining by itself does not imply endless duration.
rows.anchor: ولما كان المكث لا يقتضي التأبيد قال أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming God has a child include Jews regarding ʿUzayr, Christians regarding the Messiah, and Arabs regarding angels.
rows.anchor: والذين نسبوا الولد إلى الله تعالى بعض اليهود في عزيز

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī takes the pronoun in bihi to refer to the alleged son, making the clause an adjective of that son.
rows.anchor: قال المهدوي: فتكون الجملة صفة للولد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects describing the alleged son as the speakers intended; he treats the clause as a new divine declaration that they make the claim in ignorance.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا معترض لأنه لا يصفه إلا القائل

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī allows bihi to refer to God, a reading that indicts them even more for total ignorance.
rows.anchor: وهذا التأويل أذم لهم وأقضى في الجهل التام عليهم وهو قول الطبري

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other proposed referents for bihi are God, their utterance, or the understood act of taking a child; the last would lack knowledge of any rationale, since only the weak need an offspring as helper.
rows.anchor: قيل: والمعنى ما لهم بالله من علم فينزهوه عما لا يجوز عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks how they can lack knowledge of a son when having a child for God is inherently impossible; the reply is that an impossible matter cannot be known, whether due to an inaccessible route or its own impossibility.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: اتخاذ الله ولدا في نفسه محال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their forebears likewise had no knowledge; the descendants merely inherited this foolish claim from them by imitation.
rows.anchor: ولا لآبائهم معطوف على لهم وهم من تقدم من أسلافهم الذين ذهبوا إلى هذه المقالة السخيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read kalimatan in the accusative as specification; an unspoken subject means ‘what a great utterance,’ referring to their claim that God took a son.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: كلمة بالنصب والظاهر انتصابها على التمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following clause characterizes the word and magnifies their audacity in voicing something so atrocious, unlike evil thoughts that remain unspoken; word can name a whole poem.
rows.anchor: والجملة بعدها صفة لها تفيد استعظام اجترائهم على النطق بها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the claim is one meaning present in the mind, so it aptly counts as one word; he also analyzes the accusative like tamyīz after niʿma.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وهذه المقالة هي قائمة في النفس معنى واحدا فيحسن أن تسمى كلمة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Other grammarians take the accusative as an explanatory specification or a circumstantial, meaning the falsehood itself was great.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: نصبها على التفسير على حد نصب قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in kaburat has no antecedent before it; it is implicit and explained by the specification, or the condemned target is omitted and takhruju describes it.
rows.anchor: والضمير في كبرت ليس عائدا على ما قبله بل هو مضمر يفسره ما بعده

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda treats the construction as an exclamation meaning how great a word it is.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: نصب على التعجب أي أكبر بها كلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The b in kaburat is quiescent in a Tamimi dialect; al-Ḥasan and others read the word in the nominative as subject, while the majority’s accusative is stronger.
rows.anchor: وقرىء كبرت سكون الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inna is negative here, and kadhiban describes an omitted verbal noun: a false statement.
rows.anchor: وإن نافية أي ما يقولون وكذبا نعت لمصدر محذوف أي قولا كذبا

rows.speaker: العسكري
rows.claim: Laʿalla here is taken by al-ʿAskarī as a prohibition: do not destroy yourself.
rows.anchor: وقال العسكري: فيها هنا هي موضوعة موضع النهي يعني أن المعنى لا تبخع نفسك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some read it as an interrogative, asking whether the Prophet is about to destroy himself.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وضعت موضع الاستفهام تقديره هل أنت باخع نفسك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it a reproving reminder that means he should not be so distressed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: تقرير وتوقيف بمعنى الإنكار عليه أي لا تكن كذلك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī compares the Prophet’s grief over their rejection to a person abandoned by beloved companions, collapsing in regret and destroying himself.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: شبهه وإياهم حين تولوا عنه ولم يؤمنوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laʿalla most likely expresses fear that the Prophet might kill himself because they did not believe.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أنها للإشفاق أشفق أن يبخع الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlā āthārihim is an eloquent metaphor for their retreat and distance from belief; it means after them, after despair of belief or after their death in disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقوله على آثارهم استعارة فصيحة من حيث لهم إدبار وتباعد عن الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bākhiʿ nafsaka is read either in genitive annexation or with tanwīn and accusative; al-Zamakhsharī appeals to the normal participle government, al-Kisāʾī permits both, while the author prefers annexation as argued elsewhere.
rows.anchor: وقرىء باخع نفسك بالإضافة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads kasra in yuʾminū as an active participle referring forward and fatḥa as past under annexation.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: إن لم يؤمنوا بكسر الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hadīth means the Quran, as in the verse describing God’s revelation as the best hadīth.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بهذا الحديث إلى القرآن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid defines asaf as distress or grief.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: جزعا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda gives anger, and also transmits grief as a meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: غضبا وعنه أيضا حزنا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says asaf means regret and remorse.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: ندما وتحسرا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines asaf as extreme grief and anger.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الأسف المبالغة في الحزن والغضب

rows.speaker: منذر بن سعيد
rows.claim: Mundhir ibn Saʿīd says grief is meant when the sufferer cannot control its object, while anger applies when the object is within one’s power; he links the latter usage to 43:55.
rows.anchor: وقال منذر بن سعيد: الأسف هنا الحزن لأنه على من لا يملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asafan is accusative either as a reason or as a verbal noun used circumstantially; the next verse comforts the Prophet by explaining that earthly beauty is a test of differing deeds.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب أسفا على أنه مفعول من أجله أو على أنه مصدر في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made earthly adornment to test which people act best; not everyone follows the messengers equally, so the Prophet need not grieve, and blessings are not withdrawn even from disbelievers.
rows.anchor: لأنه تعالى أخبر أنه خلق ما على الأرض من الزينة للابتلاء والاختبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaʿalnā here means created; mā apparently refers broadly to non-rational things, and every thing has adornment suited to it.
rows.anchor: وجعلنا هنا بمعنى خلقنا، والظاهر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some exclude harmful animals, stones, and plants from adornment; defenders of the general reading say their creation, workmanship, and perfection make them beautiful.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا يدخل في ذلك ما كان فيه إيذاء من حيوان وحجر ونبات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other restricted readings identify the adornment with trees and rivers, flowering plants, animals, or precious metals and gems.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد بما هنا خصوص ما لا بعقل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī limits the phrase to worldly luxuries and attractive things fit to adorn the earth and its people.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ما على الأرض يعني ما يصلح أن يكون زينة لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous report says the adornment included blessings, clothing, fruit, greenery, and water.
rows.anchor: النعيم والملابس والثمار والخضرة والمياه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: A rational reading of mā is attributed to Mujāhid, who says it means men, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: فعن مجاهد هو الرجال وقاله ابن جبير عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says the earthly adornment means rulers, scholars, and commanders.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة أن الزينة الخلفاء والعلماء والأمراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zīnata is a circumstantial accusative or purpose object if jaʿalnā means created; if it means made into, it is the second object.
rows.anchor: وانتصب زينة على الحال أو على المفعول من أجله إن كان جعلنا بمعنى خلقنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in li-nabluwahum attaches to jaʿalnā; testing is interpreted relative to God, and hum refers to mā if rational or else the people understood from context.
rows.anchor: والابتلاء الاختبار وهو متأول بالنسبة إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyuhum may be a nominative pronoun phrase, with ahsanu as predicate and the whole question as the object of li-nabluwahum; testing is construed like knowing because it causes knowledge.
rows.anchor: فيكون أيهم مبتدأ وأحسن خبره

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī takes the clause as an interrogative sentence with a subject and predicate.
rows.anchor: وإلى أن الجملة استفهامية مبتدأ وخبر ذهب الحوفي

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Under Sībawayh’s analysis, ayyuhum may be built in the nominative because it meets the conditions for deleting the head of its relative clause; ahsanu predicates an omitted huwa, and the phrase substitutes for the pronoun in nabluwahum.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون الضمة فيها بناء على مذهب سيبويه لوجود شرط جواز البناء

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawrī says best in deeds means most ascetic toward the world.
rows.anchor: وقال الثوري أحسنهم عملا أزهدهم فيها

rows.speaker: أبو عاصم العسقلاني
rows.claim: Abū ʿĀṣim al-ʿAsqalānī says it means the one who leaves the world most readily.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عاصم العسقلاني: أترك لها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī defines good action as asceticism and avoiding delusion by worldly adornment.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: حسن العمل الزهد فيها وترك الاغترار بها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر غالب بن عطية
rows.claim: Abū Bakr Ghālib ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is taking one’s due with faith, performing obligations, avoiding prohibitions, and increasing voluntary good works.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر غالب بن عطية: أحسن العمل أخذ بحق مع الإيمان

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says best in deeds means best in obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: أحسن طاعة

rows.speaker: القاسم بن محمد
rows.claim: Al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad says the adornment includes prophets and scholars, testing which of their recipients and imitators responds and accepts best.
rows.anchor: وقال القاسم بن محمد ما عليها من الأنبياء والعلماء

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl says best action means the finest reliance on God amid worldly adornment.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل: أحسن توكلا علينا فيها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view defines the best as the purest in heart and finest in demeanor.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أصفى قلبا وأحسن سمتا

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says best means most faithful to God’s command and most active in obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق: أيهم أتبع لأمري وأعمل بطاعتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will turn what adorned the earth, or everything on it, into barren soil; this urges detachment from the world and consoles the Prophet since its beauty will perish.
rows.anchor: وهذا إشارة إلى التزهيد في الدنيا والرغبة عنها وتسلية للرسول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī pictures the earth stripped of vegetation and life, its green beauty made a bare white surface.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ما عليها من هذه الزينة صعيدا جرزا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says ṣaʿīd is ground without plants.
rows.anchor: مجاهد: الأرض التي لا نبات بها

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī defines ṣaʿīd as smooth, level ground; other views call it a road.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي الأملس المستوي. وقيل: الطريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith warns against sitting on ṣuʿud, elevated or open paths.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «إياكم والقعود على الصعدات»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Am is disconnected, equivalent to bal plus a hamza, generally marking transition rather than cancellation; some grammarians treat it as the interrogative hamza alone.
rows.anchor: أم هنا هي المنقطعة فتتقدر ببل والهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent addressee of the rhetorical question is the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في أم حسبت أنه خطاب للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the verse does not forbid amazement; rather, all God’s signs are wondrous in this way.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد: لم ينهه عن التعجب وإنما أراد كل آياتنا كذلك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says not to marvel at the youths, since creation of the heavens and earth contains greater wonders.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: لا يتعجب منها فالعجائب في خلق السموات والأرض أكثر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the questioners sought to make the answer a test of prophethood, though the Quran’s other signs are more wondrous and compelling.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: سألوك عن ذلك ليجعلوا جوابك علامة لصدقك وكذبك

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reads the question as reproaching the Prophet for regarding the cave story as uniquely astonishing when God’s other signs are greater; he attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Ibn Isḥāq.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: تقرير له عليه السلام على حسبانه أن أصحاب الكهف كانوا عجبا

rows.speaker: الزهراوي
rows.claim: Al-Zahrawī offers another reading: the question affirms that they are a wonder, prompting the Prophet to attend to their description; the wording ḥasibta is treated loosely.
rows.anchor: وقال الزهراوي: يحتمل معنى آخر وهو أن يكون استفهاما له

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say ḥasibta means ‘did you know,’ an invitation to learn that they were wondrous.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: معناه أعلمت أي لم تعلمه حتى أعلمتك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī links the question to the previous account of the earth’s adornment and its removal, contrasting that with preservation of the youths’ lives for a long time.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ذكر من الآيات الكلية تزيين الأرض بما خلق فوقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view addresses the listener or the polytheists, asking whether they thought the cave youths were a wonder.
rows.anchor: الخطاب للسامع، والمراد المشركون أي قل لهم

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas says kahf means a mountain, though the judge says this is not common usage.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس: الكهف الجبل. قال القاضي: وهذا غير مشهور في اللغة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says kahf is a cleft between two mountains.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: تفريج بين الجبلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apparently the people of the cave and al-raqīm are the same youths.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن أصحاب الكهف والرقيم هم الفتية المذكورون هنا

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib says the raqīm were another group whose situation resembled that of the cave youths.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن المسيب أنهم قوم كان حالهم كأصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk identifies al-Raqīm as a Roman town with a cave containing twenty-one dead sleepers like the cave youths.
rows.anchor: فقال الضحاك الرقيم بلدة بالروم فيها غار فيه أحد وعشرون نفسا أموات

rows.speaker: النعمان بن بشير
rows.claim: Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr reports that the Prophet told of three people trapped in a cave by a fallen rock after taking shelter from rain; their story is the account of the worker, the chaste man, and the dutiful son.
rows.anchor: ففي الحديث عن النعمان بن بشير أنه سمع الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم يذكر الرقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who distinguish two groups say the Quran reports the cave youths but says nothing about the raqīm group; those identifying one group disagree about the term’s meaning.
rows.anchor: ومن قال إنهم طائفتان قال: أخبر الله عن أصحاب الكهف ولم يخبر عن أصحاب الرقيم بشيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says he does not know whether al-raqīm means a book or a structure.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن عباس: أنه لا يدري ما الرقيم أكتاب أم بنيان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās makes al-raqīm a book containing the law by which they followed the religion of Christ, or an earlier religion.
rows.anchor: وعنه أنه كتاب كان عندهم فيه الشرع الذي تمسكوا به من دين المسيح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Wahb say al-Raqīm was the name of their town.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس ووهب أنه اسم قريتهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account calls it a golden tablet beneath a wall raised by al-Khiḍr.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لوح من ذهب تحت الجدار أقامه الخضر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other accounts say it was a tablet inscribed with their names, story, and reason for departure, or a lead tablet in a copper chest at the cave entrance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كتب فيه أسماؤهم وقصتهم وسبب خروجهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says it was a stone inscribed with their names and set into the city wall.
rows.anchor: وقيل: صخرة كتب فيها أسماؤهم وجعلت في سور المدينة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas, al-Shaʿbī, and Ibn Jubayr say al-raqīm was the dog’s name, citing Umayya’s line.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اسم كلبهم وتقدم بيت أمية قاله أنس والشعبي وابن جبير

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies al-raqīm as the mountain where the cave lay.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: الجبل الذي به الكهف

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says al-raqīm is the Roman word for an inkwell.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة اسم الدواة بالرومية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Further views make al-raqīm the valley of the cave or say people inscribed the youths’ story in the mountain.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اسم للوادي الذي فيه الكهف. وقيل: رقم الناس حديثهم نقرا في الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAjaban is an accusative adjective of an implied āyah, or an implied phrase meaning a thing of wonder.
rows.anchor: وعجبا نصب على أنه صفة لمحذوف دل عليه ما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The youths’ foreign names are uncertain in spelling and dots, transmission about their story and escape varies, and neither sound hadith nor Quran gives these details beyond the stated account.
rows.anchor: وأما أسماء فتية أهل الكهف فأعجمية لا تنضبط

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report names the pagan ruler in whose time the youths left his religion as Daqyānūs and places them among the Romans.
rows.anchor: وروي أن اسم الملك الكافر الذي خرجوا في أيامه عن ملته اسمه دقيانوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report claims that the youths were located in a cave in Syria, though neighbors identify the remains as the cave people.
rows.anchor: في الشام وأن بالشام كهفا فيه موتى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he visited the Andalusian remains in 504 AH, describing the bodies, mosque, a partly standing Roman building called al-Raqīm, and nearby ruins of Daqyūs; he records it as a lasting marvel.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: دخلت إليهم فرأيتهم منذ أربع وخمسمائة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says he repeatedly saw the ruins and heard local claims of miscounting the youths; he considers an Andalusian site more plausible given the region’s former Christian power and the remoteness of the Hijaz from these reports.
rows.anchor: ويترجح كون أهل الكهف بالأندلس لكثرة دين النصارى بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal idh is governed either by an implied udhkur or by ʿajaban; the youths made the cave a refuge and place of protection.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أوى جعلوه مأوى لهم ومكان اعتصام

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes gloss the requested mercy as provision.
rows.anchor: ثم دعوا الله تعالى أن يؤتيهم رحمة من عنده وفسرها المفسرون بالرزق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the mercy includes forgiveness, provision, and safety from enemies.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هي المغفرة والرزق والأمن من الأعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fitya is a broken plural of paucity, fitting their small number; Ibn al-Sarrāj instead calls it a collective noun, and the term indicates they were young.
rows.anchor: والفتية جمع فتى جمع تكسير جمع قلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report describes them as young Roman nobles, richly dressed with gold ornaments and sidelocks, following Jesus; another says they lived before Jesus.
rows.anchor: وكذا روي أنهم كانوا شبابا من أبناء الأشراف والعظماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Andalusian speakers commonly called Christians Rūm rather than Naṣārā; the youths ask God to grant guidance and steadiness after leaving their families’ religion for monotheism.
rows.anchor: دعوا بإيتاء الرحمة وهي تتضمن الرزق وغيره

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī glosses the prayer as making the whole affair rightly guided, like calling someone a lion.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: واجعل أمرنا رشدا كله

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and al-Zuhrī read the forms of hayyiʾ with two yāʾs and no hamza, treating this as replacement of a quiescent hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة والزهري: وهي ويهيي بياءين

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Ibn Khalawayh records al-Aʿshā’s reading from Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim without hamza; the form may reflect hamza replacement or disputed deletion, with replacement regular and deletion allowed in imperative or jussive forms.
rows.anchor: ابن خالويه الأعشى عن أبي بكر عن عاصم

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abū Rajāʾ reads rushd with ḍamma on rāʾ and a quiescent shīn; the majority read rashadan with both vowels open.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء: رشد بضم الراء وإسكان الشين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the majority reading because it resembles the surrounding verse endings; he says the prayer concerns worldly need, while the youths already trusted their afterlife guidance, though mercy could also mean the hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهي أرجح لشبهها بفواصل الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says every believer should use this sufficient prayer for worldly affairs.
rows.anchor: وينبغي لكل مؤمن أن يجعل دعاءه في أمر دنياه هذه الآية فإنها كافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Striking over their ears is a vivid metaphor for heavy sleep, conveying forceful attachment and duration; ears are named because sleep deepens when hearing is suspended.
rows.anchor: فضربنا على آذانهم استعارة بديعة للإنامة المستثقلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metaphor resembles expressions for imposed humiliation, poll tax, conscription, and qualities fixed on a person, illustrated with lines by al-Farazdaq, al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur, and an unnamed poet.
rows.anchor: وعبر بالضرب ليدل على قوة المباشرة واللصوق واللزوم ومنه ضربت عليهم الذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says Satan urinates in a man’s ear, meaning he sleeps so heavily that he does not rise at night.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «ذلك رجل بال الشيطان في أذنه»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object of ḍarabnā is a barrier that prevents hearing, as in saying one built a tent over his wife.
rows.anchor: ومفعول ضربنا محذوف أي حجابا من أن يسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinīna is a time adverb governed by ḍarabnā; ʿadadan is a verbal noun used adjectivally or with an omitted preposition, meaning counted years and suggesting many.
rows.anchor: وانتصب سنين على الظرف والعامل فيه فضربنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read linaʿlama with first-person plural; al-Zuhrī and a report in Ibn Khalawayh read it with yāʾ, and al-Akhfash also reports liyaʿlam.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور: لنعلم بالنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿathnāhum means waking them from sleep; baʿth is movement from stillness in a person or from the state in which it had been sent.
rows.anchor: ثم بعثناهم أي أيقظناهم من نومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linaʿlama means to make their already known matter manifest, as discussed for the parallel ‘so We may know who follows the Messenger.’
rows.anchor: وتقدم الكلام في نظير هذا في قوله لنعلم من يتبع الرسول

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads the verb with yāʾ; in al-Kashshāf this reading omits an object and suspends the clause as the predicate of a nominal phrase.
rows.anchor: الياء وفي كتاب ابن خالويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects al-Kashshāf’s passive-like clausal analysis under Basran grammar: a full sentence cannot serve as the substitute for an already omitted passive subject; Kufans allow either any spoken clause or only one that permits suspension.
rows.anchor: ما في الكشاف فلا يجوز ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nun reading may shift from divine first person to third-person reference without changing the meaning; with yāʾ, the omitted first object is God’s making people know which group, while the nominal clause supplies the next two objects.
rows.anchor: فأما قراءة لنعلم فيظهر أن ذلك التفات خرج من ضمير المتكلم إلى ضمير الغيبة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows ʿadadan to suggest few years because even a long period seems short to God, but the author rejects the comparison: 23:113 describes worldly life as short only when people see the promised punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ويحتمل أن يريد القلة لأن الكثير قليل عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two groups most likely are the youths themselves, as their later exchange shows; those saying the Lord knows best had realized the long duration, and the Quran first summarizes then retells the story at length.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الحزبين هما منهم لقوله تعالى وكذلك بعثناهم ليتسائلوا بينهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, reporting the majority, says one group was the youths who thought they had stayed briefly and the other was the city people who had kept a record of them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والظاهر من الآية أن الحزب الواحد هم الفتية

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the two arguing groups were Jews and Christians who prompted Quraysh to ask about the cave youths, al-Khiḍr, and the spirit; they disagreed about the duration.
rows.anchor: قال السدي من اليهود والنصارى الذين علموا قريشا السؤال عن أهل الكهف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says believers and unbelievers among the cave people disagreed about how long they stayed.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: قوم أهل الكهف كان منهم مؤمنون وكافرون

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the groups were believers living in the youths’ time, disputing the duration.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حزبان من المؤمنين في زمن أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies one group with the successive rulers of the city and the other with the cave people.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس الملوك الذين تداولوا ملك المدينة حزب وأهل الكهف حزب

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Baḥr says the two groups are God and creatures, like the question ‘Are you more knowledgeable or God?’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر: الحزبان الله والخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls these alternatives confused; Ibn Qatāda instead says neither believers nor unbelievers knew the duration, while Muqātil says waking ended the uncertainty and disclosed its truth.
rows.anchor: وهذه كلها أقوال مضطربة. وقال ابن قتادة: لم يكن للفريقين علم

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqā allow aḥṣā as a past verb with mā as a verbal noun and amadan as object, or as an elative with amadan as specification.
rows.anchor: وأحصى جوز الحوفي وأبو البقاء أن يكون فعلا ماضيا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and al-Tabrīzī prefer the elative reading; al-Fārisī, al-Zamakhsharī, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefer a past verb, citing the normal pattern for forms of comparison and exclamation.
rows.anchor: واختار الزجاج والتبريزي أن يكون أفعل للتفضيل واختار الفارسي والزمخشري وابن عطية

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says elative forms from quadriliteral verbs have become common and are therefore permissible; Ibn ʿAṭiyya misclassifies examples such as aswad and abyad, which are not quadriliteral.
rows.anchor: ويقول أبو إسحاق: إنه قد كثر من الرباعي فيجوز

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Three positions govern comparative and exclamatory afʿal: Sībawayh’s apparent view permits it freely, another allows none except anomalous forms, and a third permits it when the hamza is not causative.
rows.anchor: وفي بناء أفعل للتعجب وللتفضيل ثلاثة مذاهب يبنى منه مطلقا وهو ظاهر كلام سيبويه
